title: Nursing Process Management of Haematological Disorders

headings.title: Introduction to Haematological Disorders and the Nursing Process
headings.content: Haematological disorders encompass a wide spectrum of conditions affecting the components of blood, including red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets, and plasma proteins. Common challenges seen across Nigerian tertiary and secondary health facilities include severe anaemia secondary to malaria or nutritional deficits, sickle cell crises, and various leukaemias. Applying the nursing process provides a systematic framework to address these complex physiological and psychosocial needs. Assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, and evaluation serve as the foundational phases that guide clinical reasoning, ensuring safe and individualized care for patients facing life-altering blood pathologies.

headings.title: Comprehensive Nursing Assessment in Haematology
headings.content:
A thorough haematological assessment begins with a detailed health history, focusing on fatigue, bleeding tendencies, pain patterns, and infection history. Physical examination requires sharp observational skills: inspect the skin and mucous membranes for pallor, jaundice, petechiae, or ecchymosis. Palpate the lymph nodes, liver, and spleen to detect enlargement or tenderness. Diagnostic laboratory values demand constant scrutiny. 

- **Haemoglobin and Haematocrit**: Indicate oxygen-carrying capacity and anaemic status.
- **Platelet Count**: Guides bleeding risk evaluation and clotting efficiency.
- **White Blood Cell Differential**: Highlights underlying infection or bone marrow suppression.
- **Coagulation Studies (PT, PTT, INR)**: Monitor clotting cascade integrity, especially during anticoagulant therapy.

headings.title: Formulating Nursing Diagnoses for Blood Disorders
headings.content: Nursing diagnoses translate assessment data into actionable clinical statements that direct targeted care. In haematological disorders, alterations in tissue perfusion, risk for injury, and acute pain dominate clinical priorities. For instance, a patient experiencing severe anaemia will present with impaired tissue perfusion due to reduced oxygen delivery. When bone marrow infarction occurs during a sickle cell pain crisis, acute pain becomes a primary diagnostic focus. Accurately identifying these problems allows nurses to set clear boundaries for intervention and communicate patient status effectively across the healthcare team.

headings.title: Planning Patient-Centered Care and Goal Setting
headings.content: Planning involves establishing realistic, measurable, and time-bound goals alongside the patient and their family. In conditions like sickle cell anaemia or chronic leukaemia, goals must balance physiological stabilization with quality of life. An example of an outcome criterion is: "The patient will verbalize a pain score of less than 3 out of 10 within two hours of analgesic administration." Prioritizing care requires addressing life-threatening issues, such as active haemorrhage or profound hypoxia, before attending to comfort measures or long-term educational needs.

headings.title: Implementing Nursing Interventions for Anemia and Bleeding Disorders
headings.content: Implementation brings the care plan into action through direct physical interventions and vigilant monitoring. For patients with anaemia, energy conservation techniques, administration of prescribed hematinics, and oxygen therapy are standard. Conversely, management of bleeding disorders focuses on injury prevention: using soft toothbrushes, avoiding intramuscular injections, and minimizing venipunctures. Nurses must also watch closely for signs of internal bleeding, such as abdominal distension or unexplained drops in blood pressure, ensuring prompt escalation of care when clinical deterioration occurs.

headings.title: Managing Complications Related to Blood Transfusions and Therapy
headings.content:
Blood product administration is a high-risk therapy requiring strict adherence to safety protocols. Before starting, the nurse must verify patient identity, blood group, and unit serial numbers with a second clinician at the bedside. Vital signs are recorded baseline, 15 minutes after initiation, and hourly thereafter. 

| Transfusion Reaction Type | Key Clinical Manifestations | Immediate Nursing Action |
|---|---|---|
| **Haemolytic** | Fever, chills, lower back pain, hypotension | Stop transfusion immediately, infuse normal saline with new tubing |
| **Allergic** | Urticaria, pruritus, flushing | Slow infusion, notify physician, administer antihistamines |
| **Circulatory Overload** | Dyspnoea, orthopnoea, crackles, hypertension | Slow or stop infusion, elevate head of bed, administer diuretics |

headings.title: Patient Education and Psychosocial Support
headings.content: Living with a chronic haematological condition like sickle cell disorder or haemophilia imposes significant emotional and social burdens on patients and their families. Effective education empowers individuals to recognize early warning signs of crises, adhere to complex medication regimens, and make necessary lifestyle adjustments. In many Nigerian communities, addressing cultural beliefs and social stigmatization associated with hereditary blood disorders is just as critical as teaching physical self-care. Providing a compassionate, non-judgmental listening space helps alleviate anxiety and fosters active participation in long-term health management.

headings.title: Evaluating Nursing Outcomes and Care Effectiveness
headings.content: Evaluation is the continuous process of determining whether patient goals have been met, partially met, or unmet. The nurse reviews laboratory trends, observes physical recovery, and assesses the patient's feedback. If haemoglobin levels remain dangerously low or pain scores do not improve, the care plan must be modified. This cyclical nature of the nursing process ensures that nursing interventions remain responsive to the dynamic changes typical of haematological disorders, ultimately securing optimal clinical outcomes.
